analysis.one_liner: Requires government approval and safe handling for hazardous waste crossing US borders, and bans dumping it in Antarctica.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after a July 1991 Senate hearing, it sat in committee and the 102nd Congress ended without the Senate ever acting on it.
analysis.plain_summary: The United States had signed the Basel Convention, an international treaty requiring countries to control shipments of hazardous waste across borders. This bill would have written that treaty into US law: no company could export or import hazardous waste — or municipal trash, incinerator ash, or infectious waste — without notifying the government, getting consent from the countries involved, signing a contract for safe handling, and taking financial responsibility if a shipment went astray. It also banned sending any such waste to Antarctica and extended ocean-dumping protections to US waters. It never got a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities that host landfills, incinerators, and ports in the United States, and residents of poorer countries that have received exported US hazardous waste, would gain stronger protections against waste being shipped to wherever rules are weakest. Countries would get advance notice and a veto over waste shipments aimed at them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near waste dumps and ports

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to export or import hazardous waste — plus municipal solid waste, incinerator ash, and infectious waste — except under strict notification, consent, and contract requirements [S3].

Requires exporters to get consent from importing and transit countries before shipping, to document efforts to minimize waste, and to take legal and financial responsibility for returning waste that is not delivered or managed as agreed [S3].
Bans export of hazardous or additional waste for treatment, storage, disposal, or recycling anywhere south of 60 degrees south latitude (the Antarctic Treaty Area) [S3].

Adds criminal penalties (up to five years for knowing illegal shipments, up to fifteen for knowing endangerment), civil penalties of up to $25,000 per day, and forfeiture of property used in violations [S3].
Extends the ocean-dumping ban to the full US Exclusive Economic Zone and prohibits permits for dumping in the Antarctic Treaty Area [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Waste haulers, disposal companies, incinerator operators, and businesses that ship waste abroad would bear new notification, fee, financial-responsibility, and compliance costs, and some export routes would be barred entirely.

drawbacks.text: The compliance machinery is heavy: exporters need written contracts, multi-country consent, movement documents, annual reports, and fees, costs that could fall partly on municipal governments and businesses that generate waste [S3].

The bill gives the President wide discretion, including the power to exempt executive-branch shipments from the rules when he judges it in the paramount interest of the United States, and broad authority to bar shipments — powers that could be used loosely or selectively [S3].

Recyclable materials such as scrap metal, waste paper, and separated waste glass and plastic are excluded from most of the bill's rules, so a significant trade stream would continue with lighter oversight, subject only to the Antarctic ban [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health case is strong: untracked hazardous waste crossing borders tends to end up wherever oversight is weakest, and the bill would put notice, consent, and liability in its place. The cost is real but ordinary — paperwork, fees, and fewer cheap disposal options for waste generators — and the bill's carve-outs for recycling and the President's exemption power keep it from being as strict as a full ban. On balance the protections outweigh the compliance burden, but the bill was never tested in debate or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee, which held one hearing in July 1991, but the committee never reported it and the Senate never voted; the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. John Chafee introduced the bill on May 15, 1991, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works [S5].
The Subcommittee on Environmental Protection held hearings on July 25, 1991 — the last action the bill ever received [S5].
The bill's stated purpose was to implement the Basel Convention on controlling transboundary movements of hazardous waste, which the United States had signed in 1989 [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Waste hauling, disposal, and export businesses were better off, because they avoided the notification, fee, and liability regime the bill would have imposed. Communities abroad and near US waste facilities gained nothing, since the United States went on without Basel implementing legislation.

for.name: Sen. John Chafee
for.role: US Senator from Rhode Island (introduced the bill by request)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to implement the Basel Convention in US law; it received no cosponsors and was referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred (chaired by Sen. Quentin Burdick, D-ND)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill in May 1991 and held one subcommittee hearing in July 1991, but never reported it to the full Senate, so it never got a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors from either party, and never came to a vote, so the record shows no partisan pattern on it.

industries.industry: Hazardous and municipal waste disposal and hauling companies
industries.note: The bill would have barred most uncontrolled waste exports and imports and imposed notification, consent, contract, fee, and financial-responsibility requirements on waste shipments. These companies' business model of moving waste to the cheapest, least-regulated destination would have been constrained.

Recyclable streams — scrap metal, waste paper, waste glass and plastic separated from municipal waste — were excluded from most of the bill's rules, so the core export trade would have continued largely untouched, subject only to the Antarctic ban.

industries.industry: Ports and ocean shipping of waste
industries.note: The bill extended the ocean-dumping prohibition to the full US Exclusive Economic Zone and banned permits for dumping in the Antarctic Treaty Area, tightening rules for waste transported by sea while letting the President restrict waste shipments to designated ports.
